title: The Essays
alternative_titles: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
description: Francis Bacon's essays, published in three successively enlarged editions (ten essays in 1597, thirty-eight in 1612, fifty-eight in 1625): counsels civil and moral on studies, truth, death, revenge, marriage, gardens, masques, and the conduct of public life, in the aphoristic prose that made the form an English genre.
plot_or_argument: No plot: each essay is a compact meditation on its subject — the 1625 title calls them 'counsels, civil and moral' — moving from observation through maxim to practical advice, with the famous 'Of Studies' ('Reading maketh a full man') and 'Of Truth' as its touchstones.
narrative_structure: A collection of fifty-eight numbered essays in the final edition, each a self-contained meditation in the Senecan and Montaignian modes.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of aphoristic compression — antithesis, balance, and the telling image — deliberately plain and packed.
historical_context: The 1597 edition was among the first English essay collections, after Florio's Montaigne was still to come; the 1625 edition, published the year before Bacon's death, is the canonical text and the foundation of the English essay tradition.
literary_significance: The book that naturalized the essay in English — the prose counterpart of Bacon's philosophical revolution, and a schoolbook of English style for three centuries.
bibliographical_notes: Editions of 1597, 1612, and 1625. Standard edition: Michael Kiernan (ed.), The Essayes or Counsels, Civill and Morall (Oxford, 1985).

title: The Advancement of Learning
alternative_titles: The Two Books of Francis Bacon of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, Divine and Human
description: Bacon's great survey and defence of knowledge, addressed to James I: the first book vindicates learning against its 'distempers' and detractors; the second maps the whole territory of human knowledge — history, poesy, and philosophy, with their divisions and gaps — in the programme that the Latin De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623) would expand.
plot_or_argument: Book I argues the dignity and utility of learning against the objections of divines, politicians, and the learned themselves; Book II proceeds through the three faculties of memory, imagination, and reason, charting each science, noting its deficiencies, and closing with the practical counsel for the advancement of knowledge in Bacon's own time.
narrative_structure: Two books of systematic argument — apology, then map — in the humanist tradition of the treatise addressed to a prince.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of sustained periodic power, with the famous catalogue of the impediments to learning.
historical_context: Published in 1605, in the first years of James I's reign, as Bacon's bid for the role of philosophical counsellor; it is the seed of the Instauratio Magna and the later Latin works.
literary_significance: The founding charter of English scientific and philosophical prose — the map of knowledge that organized the intellectual world until the Encyclopedists.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for Henry Tomes, 1605. Standard edition: The Oxford Francis Bacon, vol. 4, ed. Michael Kiernan (2000).

title: Novum Organum
description: Bacon's second part of the Instauratio Magna, published in Latin: the 'New Instrument' of science, in which the old logic of Aristotle is replaced by the new method of induction — the doctrine of the idols (of the tribe, cave, marketplace, and theatre), the tables of presence and absence, and the 'prerogative instances' that guide the interpretation of nature.
plot_or_argument: Book I clears the ground: the idols that beset the mind, the signs of philosophy's failure, and the hope of a new beginning; Book II lays out the method — the tables of instances, the first vintage, and the ascending ladder of axioms that ends in the knowledge of forms and the power over nature ('knowledge and human power are synonymous').
narrative_structure: Two books of aphorisms, deliberately fragmentary, in the oracular style Bacon devised for his philosophical testament.
meter_and_prosody: Latin aphorisms of epigrammatic force, with the prefatory matter framing the work as the 'second part' of the Instauratio.
historical_context: Published in 1620, the year of the Mayflower, as the manifesto of the new experimental science; Bacon's idols doctrine became the common vocabulary of seventeenth-century epistemology.
literary_significance: The founding document of the scientific method — the text that named the idols and invented induction as the modern world understands it.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by John Bill, 1620. Standard edition: The Oxford Francis Bacon, vol. 11, ed. Graham Rees (2004).

title: New Atlantis
description: Bacon's unfinished utopian fable, published posthumously with Sylva Sylvarum: a ship lost in the Pacific reaches the unknown island of Bensalem, where the narrator is received into a society organized around Salomon's House — the college of the 'Merchants of Light' whose institutes of experiment and invention anticipate the modern research laboratory.
plot_or_argument: The sailors' arrival, the quarantine, and the Feast of the Family occupy the early pages; the governor's account of Bensalem's Christian origins and its concealment from the world follows; and the narrative climaxes in the Father of Salomon's House describing the college's 'preparations and instruments' — the prolongation of life, the making of new species, the knowledge of causes and secret motions of things.
narrative_structure: A utopian narrative in the Platonic and Morean tradition, unfinished, ending on the Father's promise that the narrator shall receive 'a relation of the true state of Salomon's House'.
principal_characters: the narrator; the Governor of the Strangers' House; the Father of Salomon's House; Joabin; the sailors
meter_and_prosody: Prose of ceremonial dignity, with the Father's discourse as the work's set piece.
historical_context: Written about 1624, in Bacon's last years at Gorhambury, and published by William Rawley in 1627; its Bensalem answered More's Utopia and anticipated the Royal Society, which took Salomon's House as its inspiration.
literary_significance: The great English utopia of science — the blueprint of the modern research institution and the ancestor of the scientific romance.
bibliographical_notes: Printed with Sylva Sylvarum by William Rawley, 1627. Standard edition: The Oxford Francis Bacon, vol. 3, ed. Michael Kiernan (2000).

title: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity
description: Hooker's great defence of the Elizabethan church: Books I–IV (1593) and Book V (1597) of the eight-book treatise answer the Puritan platform by grounding church order in the law of reason and nature — the famous account of law's hierarchy from God through angels and man to the laws ecclesiastical — in the prose that founded Anglican theology.
plot_or_argument: Book I derives the kinds of law (eternal, celestial, natural, human, divine) and the necessity of law for the good life; Books II–IV refute the Puritan claim of scriptural exclusivity; Book V, the longest, defends the Prayer Book's liturgy, sacraments, and discipline against the Admonition controversies; the posthumous Books VI–VIII treat jurisdiction, episcopacy, and royal supremacy.
narrative_structure: Eight books of systematic theological argument, each built on the scholastic method of position, objection, and answer, in the majestic periodic prose Hooker perfected.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of unrivalled dignity and clarity — the 'judicious' style that Izaak Walton celebrated and that set the standard for English theological writing.
historical_context: Written through the 1590s against the Admonition controversy and the Presbyterian challenge; the completed books were printed in 1593 and 1597, with the later books posthumous and textually vexed.
literary_significance: The intellectual foundation of Anglicanism and of the English theory of law and consent — a book Locke and the constitutional tradition built upon.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the posthumous books VI–VIII survive in imperfect texts.
bibliographical_notes: Books I–IV, 1593; Book V, 1597. Standard edition: The Folger Library Edition of the Works of Richard Hooker, gen. ed. W. Speed Hill (1977–98).

title: Actes and Monuments
description: John Foxe's 'Book of Martyrs': the vast church history and martyrology, first published in English in 1563 and expanded in 1570, tracing the true church from the apostles through Wyclif and the Lollards to the Protestant martyrs of Mary's reign — Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and hundreds more — with their examinations and burnings recorded in documentary detail and vivid woodcuts.
plot_or_argument: The work moves from the early church through the medieval persecutions to the Marian burnings; each martyrdom is given its examinations, letters, and death-scene; the 1570 edition's calendar of martyrs and its apparatus made the book a national monument as well as a history.
narrative_structure: A documentary martyrology in the tradition of Eusebius, organized chronologically by reign, with the records of trials and letters embedded in the narrative.
principal_characters: Thomas Cranmer; Hugh Latimer; Nicholas Ridley; John Wyclif; John Rogers; the Marian martyrs
meter_and_prosody: Prose of documentary accumulation, with the set-piece death scenes (Latimer's 'we shall this day light such a candle') as its rhetorical peaks.
historical_context: First English edition 1563, expanded 1570; ordered by Convocation to be placed in every cathedral church; its account of the Marian burnings shaped English Protestant identity for three centuries.
literary_significance: The most influential book of the English Reformation after the Bible itself — the founding text of English Protestant memory.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by John Day, 1563; enlarged 1570. Standard edition: The Acts and Monuments Online (University of Sheffield/HRI, 2011).

title: A Mirror for Magistrates
description: The great Elizabethan collection of 'complaints', planned by Thomas Sackville and others as a continuation of Lydgate's Fall of Princes: the ghosts of England's fallen rulers and nobles — from Albanact and Cordila to Richard III and the Duke of Buckingham — rise before the poets and tell their tragedies, warning magistrates against ambition, flattery, and misrule; Sackville's own 'Induction' and 'Complaint of Buckingham' crown the 1563 edition.
plot_or_argument: In Sackville's Induction, the poet descends with Sorrow into the underworld and meets the train of the fallen; each ghost then speaks his or her complaint — the causes of the fall anatomized in de casibus form — in poems by Sackville, Baldwin, Ferrers, Churchyard, and others across the successive editions.
narrative_structure: A frame (the poets meeting to continue Lydgate) enclosing a series of dramatic monologues by the ghosts of the great, in the medieval de casibus tradition revived for Tudor statecraft.
principal_characters: Sorrow; the poet; the ghosts of Richard III, the Duke of Buckingham, Jane Shore, Cardinal Wolsey, Lord Hastings, the Black Prince, and many others
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal and varied stanzas, with Sackville's Induction in his stateliest blank verse and rhyme.
historical_context: The first edition (1559) was suppressed for its treatment of living magnates; the fuller editions of 1563 and later became the storehouse of plots and moral themes for the Elizabethan history play.
literary_significance: The great poetic quarry of Elizabethan tragedy — the book Shakespeare, Marlowe, and the chroniclers all mined for their falls of princes.
attribution_notes: Collaborative, planned by Sackville and written chiefly by William Baldwin and George Ferrers, with Sackville's Induction and Buckingham; individual attributions follow the early editions.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1559; enlarged 1563. Standard edition: The Mirror for Magistrates, ed. Lily B. Campbell (Cambridge, 1938).

title: The Steel Glass
description: Gascoigne's satirical mirror poem: renouncing the flattering crystal of courtly verse, the poet holds up the 'steel glass' of truth to every estate — kings, knights, clergy, lawyers, merchants, and ploughmen — in the first original English poem in blank verse, its plain style answering its plain purpose.
plot_or_argument: The poet's glass shows each estate its vices: the king's flatterers, the soldier's greed, the lawyer's delays, the merchant's falsehood, and the farmer's honest toil praised last and most; the poem ends with the satirist's defence of his plain dealing and his glass's unflattering truth.
narrative_structure: A single continuous satire in the estates tradition, ordered by rank from court to country, with the glass as its governing emblem.
principal_characters: the poet; the estates personified (kings, knights, clergy, lawyers, merchants, ploughmen)
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse — the first original English poem in the form — in the plain style its argument demands.
historical_context: Published in 1576, in Gascoigne's final year, with the woodcut frontispiece of the author; it answered the court's demand for moral counsel in the decade of the Northern Rebellion's aftermath.
literary_significance: The first original blank-verse poem in English and the bridge between medieval estates satire and Elizabethan satire proper.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for Richard Smith, 1576. Standard edition: The Complete Works of George Gascoigne, ed. John W. Cunliffe, 2 vols (Cambridge, 1907–10).

title: The Adventures of Master F.J.
alternative_titles: A Discourse of the Adventures Passed by Master F.J.
description: Gascoigne's prose fiction of seduction, printed in A Hundred Sundry Flowers (1573): the gallant F.J., a guest in a northern castle, conducts an affair with the lady Elinor — their letters, verses, and assignations documented in the narrative's self-conscious apparatus — until the affair sours into jealousy, betrayal, and the narrator's moralizing close; the first English novel of intrigue, revised and bowdlerized in The Posies (1575).
plot_or_argument: F.J. arrives at the castle, courts Elinor by letter and verse; the affair progresses through the night meetings and the gift of the sword; the secretary's treachery and Elinor's inconstancy turn love to jealousy; and the narrator's apparatus — the editor's letters and comments — frames the tale as 'translated' from Italian and morally cautioned.
narrative_structure: A framed novella with the editorial machinery of letters, verses, and marginal commentary — the first English fiction to flaunt its own making.
principal_characters: Master F.J.; Elinor; the secretary; Dame Frances; the narrator-editor (G.T.)
meter_and_prosody: Prose with interpolated verses, in the manner of the Italian novella and the French Heptameron tradition.
historical_context: Printed in 1573 and revised in The Posies (1575) after the scandal of its supposed real-life originals; it anticipated the psychological fiction of the next century by a generation.
literary_significance: The first original English novel of manners — the seed of the English tradition of prose fiction that runs through Deloney and Nashe to Defoe.
bibliographical_notes: In A Hundred Sundry Flowers, 1573. Standard edition: The Complete Works of George Gascoigne, ed. John W. Cunliffe (Cambridge, 1907–10).

title: Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit
description: Lyly's first Euphues book and the fountain of Euphuism: the young Athenian Euphues comes to Naples, where the friendship with Philautus, the love of Lucilla, and her inconstancy teach him the anatomy of wit — the whole told in the balanced, antithetical, simile-laden prose that took England by storm and gave the decade its style.
plot_or_argument: Euphues wins Philautus's friendship and then Lucilla's love, betraying his friend; Lucilla's fickleness (she turns to Curio) punishes the traitor; the debate on love, the letters of counsel, and Euphues's departure close the book with the moral anatomy — 'wit' dissected into its deceits and remedies.
narrative_structure: A moral romance in the manner of the Italian questioni d'amore: narrative framed by debate, letters, and the concluding 'Cooling Card' against love.
principal_characters: Euphues; Philautus; Lucilla; Curio; the old gentleman of Naples; the ladies of Naples
meter_and_prosody: Prose of elaborate Euphuistic balance — antithesis, isocolon, and the zoological similes of Pliny's natural history.
historical_context: Published in 1578 and reprinted a dozen times by 1600; the style it founded was imitated by Greene, Lodge, and the court, and parodied by Shakespeare and Nashe within the decade.
literary_significance: The most influential prose style of the English Renaissance — the book that taught a generation to write, and to think in balances.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for Gabriel Cawood, 1578. Standard edition: The Complete Works of John Lyly, ed. R. Warwick Bond (Oxford, 1902).

title: Euphues and His England
description: Lyly's sequel: Euphues and his friend Philautus sail for England, where the courtship of the ladies — Camilla, Surius's sister, and the rest — and the praises of Elizabeth I, the English court, and English women fill the book, in the second and final installment of the Euphuistic diptych.
plot_or_argument: The voyage, the arrival in Dover, and the tour of England's marvels frame the main action: Philautus courts the ladies, Euphues plays the counsellor, and the long debate on love, beauty, and constancy ends with the famous 'glass for Europe' — the encomium of Queen Elizabeth that closes the book.
narrative_structure: A travel frame enclosing the courtship debates, letters, and the concluding praise of England, mirroring the first book's structure.
principal_characters: Euphues; Philautus; Camilla; Lady Flavia; Surius; Fidus; Psellus; Queen Elizabeth (praised in the encomium)
meter_and_prosody: The Euphuistic prose at its ripest, with the encomium of Elizabeth as its set piece.
historical_context: Published in 1580, the year of Drake's circumnavigation and the Jesuit mission's arrival; its celebration of England answered the national mood and fixed Euphues as the English style's patron.
literary_significance: The completion of the Euphuistic diptych and a founding text of English literary nationalism.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for Gabriel Cawood, 1580. Standard edition: The Complete Works of John Lyly, ed. R. Warwick Bond (Oxford, 1902).

title: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil
description: Nashe's first great pamphlet: Pierce Penniless, a scholar out of money and patience, writes his supplication to the devil, anatomizing the seven deadly sins as the diseases of London — greed, drunkenness, pride, and the rest — with the famous digression on the 'upstart' playwrights and the defence of poetry, in the fastest prose of the decade.
plot_or_argument: Pierce, penniless, petitions the devil through the knight of the post; his catalogue of sins prosecutes each vice with its London specimens — the usurer, the drunkard, the proud courtier — and the digressions on players and poets mount the first defence of the professional writer's trade.
narrative_structure: A mock-oration in the complaint tradition — the supplication as satirical frame — with the sin-catalogue and the digressions as its bravura set pieces.
principal_characters: Pierce Penniless; the Devil; the Knight of the Post; the personified sins; the poet and the player (in the digression)
meter_and_prosody: Prose of furious energy — colloquial, learned, and comic by turns — with the famous passage on the theatre's power.
historical_context: Published 1592 in the plague year; its satire of the sins and its praise of the stage (the passage on Talbot in Henry VI) made it the talk of London and fixed Nashe's reputation.
literary_significance: The great satirical pamphlet of the 1590s — the prose in which the Elizabethan town found its voice and its conscience.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Jones, 1592. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Nashe, ed. R. B. McKerrow, 5 vols (1904–10; rev. F. P. Wilson, 1958).

title: The Unfortunate Traveller
description: Nashe's picaresque novel: the page Jack Wilton travels through the wars and cities of Europe — tricking the camp at Tergou, fleeing the sweating sickness and the plague, witnessing the massacre of the Anabaptists at Münster, courting in Italy, and escaping the rape-and-execution plot of the Jew Zadoch and the courtesan Juliana — in the first English novel of adventure and the grotesque.
plot_or_argument: Jack's tricks in the army, his travels with the Earl of Surrey (and the Italian Diamante in boy's disguise), the horrors of Münster and of plague-struck Rome, the anatomies and executions, and the final escape through the villain's own engines carry the narrative to its abrupt, comic close.
narrative_structure: A first-person travel narrative in the manner of Lazarillo de Tormes, episodic and sensational, with the set pieces of horror (the anatomies, the executions) as its climaxes.
principal_characters: Jack Wilton; the Earl of Surrey; Diamante; Zadoch; Zachary; Juliana; the Pope; Heraclide; the Anabaptists
meter_and_prosody: Prose of Nashe's most violent invention — the grotesque, the comic, and the lyrical in rapid succession.
historical_context: Published 1594; its continental horrors answered the decade's appetite for travel lies and martyrdom pamphlets, and its Italian scenes the anti-Catholic mood.
literary_significance: The first English picaresque novel — the ancestor of Defoe, Smollett, and the English novel's roguish line.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Thomas Scarlet, 1594. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Nashe, ed. R. B. McKerrow (1904–10; rev. F. P. Wilson, 1958).

title: Christ's Tears over Jerusalem
description: Nashe's plague-year pamphlet: Christ's prophecy of Jerusalem's fall becomes a sermon on London's sins — usury, pride, and the city's feasting amid the plague — with the famous address to the 'adulterous and sinful' city and the appended 'Tears over London'; the book that made Nashe feared as a prophet and jailed for its satire.
plot_or_argument: The opening visions of Jerusalem's destruction give way to the anatomy of London's sins: the merchants' frauds, the gallants' pride, the women's painting; the closing 'Tears' plead for repentance before the plague's judgment, with the whole framed as Christ's lament applied to the present city.
narrative_structure: A sermon-pamphlet in the complaint tradition — biblical exegesis turned urban satire, with the visionary frame and the moral application.
principal_characters: Christ (as speaker); Jerusalem; London; the personified sins
meter_and_prosody: Prose of pulpit rhetoric crossed with the pamphlet's street energy — the style that made Nashe the most imitated and most dangerous writer of the plague years.
historical_context: Published 1593, in the worst plague year of the decade, when the theatres were closed and the authorities edgy; the satire on the city's magistrates landed Nashe in the Fleet prison.
literary_significance: The great plague literature of the 1590s — the pamphlet that turned the biblical lament into an instrument of urban satire.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for John Danter, 1593. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Nashe, ed. R. B. McKerrow (1904–10; rev. F. P. Wilson, 1958).

title: Pandosto
description: Greene's romance of jealousy and recognition, subtitled 'The Triumph of Time': King Pandosto of Bohemia, seized by groundless jealousy of his queen Bellaria and his friend King Egistus, destroys his family; the lost daughter Fawnia grows up a shepherd's daughter, is wooed by Egistus's son Dorastus, and the final recognitions restore her — though Pandosto's own suicide shadows the happy ending; the direct source of Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.
plot_or_argument: Pandosto's jealousy kills Bellaria and exposes the infant Fawnia; the shepherds raise her; Dorastus loves her despite his father's opposition; the lovers flee to Bohemia, where the recognition scene discloses Fawnia's birth; the marriages are made — and Pandosto, overcome, kills himself, the 'triumph of time' his epitaph.
narrative_structure: A prose romance in the Greek manner — jealousy, exposure, pastoral, recognition — with the oracles and storms as its machinery.
principal_characters: Pandosto; Bellaria; Egistus; Fawnia; Dorastus; the shepherd Porrus; Capnio
meter_and_prosody: Prose of Greene's pastoral sweetness, with the euphuistic balance softened into narrative flow.
historical_context: Published 1588; it went through many editions as 'Pandosto' and 'Dorastus and Fawnia', and supplied Shakespeare with the plot, names, and even phrases of The Winter's Tale.
literary_significance: The romance that became The Winter's Tale — the most consequential of the Elizabethan prose fictions by its afterlife.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Thomas Orwin, 1588. Standard edition: The Life and Complete Works in Prose and Verse of Robert Greene, ed. Alexander B. Grosart, 15 vols (1881–86).

title: Menaphon
description: Greene's pastoral romance: the shepherd Menaphon, the disguised princess Sephestia and her son, and the rival suitors of Arcadia play out the loves, riddles, and recognitions of the pastoral world, with the inserted eclogues and the story of the treacherous Samela — the whole prefaced by Thomas Nashe's address 'To the Gentlemen Students', with its famous survey of the English poets.
plot_or_argument: Sephestia, shipwrecked and disguised as Samela, is wooed by the shepherd Menaphon, the courtier Melicertus (her own husband in disguise), and the tyrant Democles; the oracles, the riddles of parentage, and the final recognitions restore the royal family, with the eclogues and debates of the shepherds as interludes.
narrative_structure: A prose romance with verse eclogues in the Sidneyan manner, prefaced by Nashe's critical epistle — one of the key documents of Elizabethan literary self-consciousness.
principal_characters: Menaphon; Sephestia (Samela); Melicertus (Maximius); Democles; the child Pleusidippus; Doron; Carmela
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the pastoral mode with interpolated verse, in Greene's most polished Arcadian style.
historical_context: Published 1589, in the wake of Sidney's Arcadia's manuscript fame; Nashe's preface praises Sidney, Spenser, and the new poetry and dismisses the 'deep read grammarians' — a manifesto of the 1590s avant-garde.
literary_significance: The best of Greene's Arcadian romances and the vehicle of Nashe's manifesto — the first public statement of the new Elizabethan literary generation.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; Nashe's preface is his own.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Thomas Orwin, 1589. Standard edition: The Life and Complete Works of Robert Greene, ed. Alexander B. Grosart (1881–86).

title: Jack of Newbury
alternative_titles: The Pleasant History of John Winchcomb
description: Deloney's fiction of the clothier's golden age: John Winchcomb of Newbury rises from apprentice to the greatest clothier in England, his hundred looms employing hundreds, his wealth commanding kings, and his virtue (he feeds the poor, arms his men for Flodden, refuses a knighthood) making him the hero of England's craftsmen — the first English novel of the working world.
plot_or_argument: Jack's rise, his marriage to his late master's widow, the great household of the looms, the visit of Queen Katherine, the expedition to Flodden, and the pranks of the courtiers against the honest clothier fill the episodic narrative, which closes on his death and the praise of his charity.
narrative_structure: An episodic biography in the jest-book and chronicle manner, built of set pieces — the banquet, the expedition, the courtiers' gulling — in the popular prose Deloney perfected.
principal_characters: Jack (John Winchcomb); his wife (the widow); Queen Katherine; King Henry VIII; the courtiers; the clothiers of England
meter_and_prosody: Plain, vigorous prose with interpolated songs and ballads, in the speech of shop and street.
historical_context: Published 1597, in the decade of the cloth trade's crisis and the apprentices' unrest; its celebration of the clothier's charity answered the dearth and the poor laws with fiction.
literary_significance: The first great novel of English working life — the book that gave the artisan class its own literature, and the ancestor of the industrial novel.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by John Danter, 1597. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Deloney, ed. Francis Oscar Mann (Oxford, 1912).

title: The Gentle Craft
description: Deloney's fiction of the shoemakers' craft: the legendary origins of the 'gentle craft' in the saints and heroes who took up shoemaking — St Hugh, St Crispin and Crispianus, Sir Simon Eyre the shoemaker Lord Mayor, and the apprentice who married a king's daughter — the book that gave Dekker his Shoemaker's Holiday and the trade its mythology.
plot_or_argument: The frame of the shoemakers' feast encloses the tales: Hugh's love for the king's daughter Winifred and his martyrdom; Crispin and Crispianus serving the king in disguise; Simon Eyre's rise to the mayoralty; and the apprentice Tom Drum's wooing of a great lady — each tale proving the craft's gentility and the shoemaker's wit.
narrative_structure: A frame-tale collection in the manner of the Decameron, with each story a romance or jest of the craft's legends.
principal_characters: St Hugh; Winifred; St Crispin; Crispianus; Simon Eyre; Tom Drum; the master shoemakers and their guests
meter_and_prosody: Prose of Deloney's popular register, with songs and the frame's festive setting.
historical_context: Published about 1597–98; its Eyre story supplied the plot of Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), and its craft-patriotism answered the decade's civic pride.
literary_significance: The classic of the craft romance — the book that made the shoemaker's bench a seat of English legend.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for Ralph Blower, c. 1597–98. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Deloney, ed. Francis Oscar Mann (Oxford, 1912).

title: Rosalynde
description: Lodge's pastoral romance, the direct source of Shakespeare's As You Like It: Rosader (Orlando), disinherited by his brother, flees to the forest of Arden, where the banished king, the disguised Rosalynde, and the shepherds' loves play out the courtships, disguises, and recognitions of the greenwood — the whole styled 'Euphues' golden legacy' and salted with eclogues.
plot_or_argument: Saladyne's cruelty drives Rosader to the forest; Rosalynde, banished by the usurper Torismond, walks there disguised as Ganymede; the lovers' meetings in disguise, the lion's attack, the rescue of Saladyne, and the final scene's restorations — the true king, the brothers, and the three marriages — close the romance in Arden's court.
narrative_structure: A prose romance of exile and disguise in the pastoral mode, with verse eclogues and the euphuistic style of its subtitle.
principal_characters: Rosader; Rosalynde (Ganymede); Saladyne; Alinda (Aliena); Torismond; Gerismond the exiled king; Phoebe; Montanus; Corydon; Adam Spencer
meter_and_prosody: Euphuistic prose with pastoral verse, in Lodge's sweetest and most musical register.
historical_context: Published 1590, at the height of the pastoral vogue; Shakespeare followed its plot closely in As You Like It (1599), keeping the forest, the disguises, and even the names of Phoebe and Adam.
literary_significance: The pastoral romance that became one of Shakespeare's greatest comedies — the greenwood's prose and the stage's poetry in one tradition.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Thomas Orwin, 1590. Standard edition: Rosalynde, ed. Brian Nellist (in Elizabethan Prose Fiction, 1968).

title: The Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffics and Discoveries of the English Nation
description: Hakluyt's great collection of English voyage narratives: the documents of the nation's seafaring — from the voyages of the Cabots and the Muscovy Company through Hawkins, Drake, and Frobisher to Ralegh's Virginia and the East India voyages — gathered, translated, and arranged in the first edition of 1589 and the vastly expanded three-volume second edition of 1598–1600.
plot_or_argument: No single plot: the collection proceeds by region and voyage, each narrative a first-hand account — ship's journals, letters, treaties, and reports — of the discovery, trade, and plunder by which England measured the globe.
narrative_structure: A documentary anthology organized geographically (north, south, east) and chronologically, with Hakluyt's prefaces and dedications providing the patriotic frame.
principal_characters: the voyagers (Sebastian Cabot, John Hawkins, Francis Drake, Martin Frobisher, Walter Ralegh, and hundreds of others)
meter_and_prosody: Prose of many hands, edited by Hakluyt into the great prose epic of English expansion.
historical_context: First edition 1589; the three-volume second edition appeared 1598–1600, in the years of the Armada's aftermath and the East India Company's founding; the collection became the sourcebook of English colonialism.
literary_significance: The 'prose epic of the modern English nation' (Froude) — the book that taught England the world's geography and its own imperial vocation.
attribution_notes: Compiled and edited by Hakluyt; the individual narratives are by many authors, credited within the work.
bibliographical_notes: First edition, 1589; second edition, 3 vols, 1598–1600. Standard edition: The Principal Navigations, ed. Jack Beeching (Penguin, 1972, selection).

title: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Beautiful Empire of Guiana
description: Ralegh's report of his 1595 voyage up the Orinoco in search of the fabled golden empire of El Dorado: the rivers, peoples, and wonders of Guiana described with the eyewitness's precision and the courtier's art, the gold of Manoa promised and half-believed, and the whole offered to Elizabeth I as the instrument of Spain's overthrow.
plot_or_argument: The narrative follows the expedition from Trinidad up the Orinoco's mouths; the Indian peoples, the Spanish depredations, the rumours of Manoa's gold, and the hardships of the return fill the account, which closes with Ralegh's arguments for the conquest of Guiana and his answers to the objections of the envious.
narrative_structure: A first-person voyage narrative with the apparatus of argument and apology — the explorer's report fused with the promoter's prospectus.
principal_characters: Sir Walter Ralegh (the narrator); the Indian peoples of the Orinoco; Topiawari (the aged cacique); the Spanish governor Berreo; the expedition's captains
meter_and_prosody: Prose of grave, plain magnificence — the Elizabethan traveller's style at its finest.
historical_context: Published 1596 after the 1595 voyage; its promise of El Dorado underwrote Ralegh's career, his 1617 return voyage, and his death.
literary_significance: The classic English narrative of exploration — the book that fixed El Dorado in the European imagination.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Robert Robinson, 1596. Standard edition: The Discoverie of Guiana, ed. Neil L. Whitehead (Manchester, 1997).

title: The History of the World
description: Ralegh's great history, written during his imprisonment in the Tower: the story of the world from the Creation to the end of the Macedonian empire, told as the record of God's providence over kingdoms — with the famous preface's meditation on death ('O eloquent, just, and mighty Death!') and the running argument that the wise man serves God, not fortune.
plot_or_argument: The five books move from the Creation and the patriarchs through Egypt, Assyria, and Persia to Greece and Alexander; the rise and fall of each empire demonstrates the providence that raises and casts down; and the closing books and the preface frame the whole as counsel to princes and consolation to the prisoner.
narrative_structure: A universal chronicle in the classical and biblical tradition, organized by empire, with the author's moral reflections interlacing the narrative.
principal_characters: Adam; Noah; Moses; the kings of Egypt, Assyria, and Persia; Alexander the Great; the historical actors of the five books
meter_and_prosody: Prose of grave sententiousness — the prison's composure in every period.
historical_context: Written 1603–14 in the Tower, dedicated to Prince Henry, and published in 1614; James I is said to have disliked it as 'too saucy in censuring princes', and the book was suppressed after Ralegh's fall.
literary_significance: The great English history of the Renaissance — the prisoner's summa of providence and power that Milton and Cromwell's generation read as scripture of state.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Stansby for Walter Burre, 1614. Standard edition: The History of the World, ed. C. A. Patrides (Macmillan, 1971, selection).

title: The Essays of Montaigne
description: John Florio's translation of Montaigne's Essays (1603), made from the 1595 French edition: the first complete English Montaigne, in which the Frenchman's scepticism, self-portraiture, and humane wisdom enter English prose in Florio's expansive, inventive idiom — the book Shakespeare read and quarried for The Tempest.
plot_or_argument: No plot: the Essays proceed by subject — custom, cannibals, coaches, friendship, experience — Montaigne's 'I' the matter of the book, and Florio's version enlarging the French into the rich Elizabethan English of the translator's own invention.
narrative_structure: Three books of essays in the 1595 arrangement, with Florio's dedicatory epistles, his preface 'To the Reader', and his appendix of the author's life.
principal_characters: Michel de Montaigne (as speaker); his friend La Boétie (in 'Of Friendship'); the cannibals; the ancients quoted throughout
meter_and_prosody: Prose of Florio's characteristic copiousness — Montaigne's sentences doubled and ornamented into the idiom that Shakespeare knew.
historical_context: Published 1603, dedicated to the Countess of Bedford and others; Shakespeare's Gonzalo in The Tempest paraphrases 'Of Cannibals' from this translation, the most famous borrowing in English drama.
literary_significance: One of the great translations in the language — the book that gave English thought its sceptical conscience and Shakespeare his New World speech.
attribution_notes: Translation by John Florio from the 1595 French text; uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Edward Blount, 1603. Standard edition: Florio's Montaigne, ed. Stephen Greenblatt and Peter G. Platt (New York Review Books, 2014).

title: Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
alternative_titles: The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
description: Sir Thomas North's translation of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, made from Jacques Amyot's French (1559): the paired biographies of the Greek and Roman great — Theseus and Romulus, Alexander and Caesar, Coriolanus and Alcibiades, Antony and Demetrius, and the rest — in the full, energetic English prose that became Shakespeare's quarry for Julius Caesar, Coriolanus, Antony and Cleopatra, and Timon of Athens.
plot_or_argument: Each pair of lives narrates its heroes' births, deeds, and deaths with the parallel moral comparisons; the collection as a whole is a gallery of virtue and vice in action — the school of statesmen and the storehouse of tragedy.
narrative_structure: The paired lives in the Amyot order, with the comparisons of the pairs and North's dedication to Queen Elizabeth.
principal_characters: Theseus; Romulus; Alexander; Julius Caesar; Coriolanus; Alcibiades; Mark Antony; Demetrius; the Greek and Roman worthies
meter_and_prosody: Prose of dramatic vividness and copiousness — Shakespeare followed its phrasing so closely that whole speeches of the Roman plays are North's sentences re-lined as verse.
historical_context: Published 1579, in the decade of the English Plutarch vogue; it went through editions in 1595, 1603, and beyond, and was the most-read secular book of the Elizabethan age after the chronicles.
literary_significance: The most consequential translation of the English Renaissance — the book through which Plutarch's heroes became Shakespeare's Romans.
attribution_notes: Translation by North from Amyot's French; uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Thomas Vautrollier, 1579. Standard edition: Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (Shakespeare Head Press, 1928).

title: Ovid's Metamorphoses
alternative_titles: The XV Books of P. Ovidius Naso, Entitled Metamorphosis
description: Arthur Golding's complete translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses (the first four books in 1565, all fifteen in 1567): the myths of transformation — Daphne, Actaeon, Narcissus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Medea, and the rest — rendered in rollicking rhymed fourteeners with a Puritan's moralizing commentary, the version that was 'Shakespeare's Ovid' and the Renaissance Englishman's classic.
plot_or_argument: The fifteen books run from the Creation through the myths of gods and mortals, metamorphosis by metamorphosis, to the apotheosis of Caesar; Golding's translation adds the epistle and preface that turn the pagan fables into allegories of divine and moral truth.
narrative_structure: The fifteen books of Ovid in order, with Golding's prefatory apparatus (the epistle to Leicester and the preface to the reader) framing the whole.
principal_characters: Jupiter; Apollo; Daphne; Actaeon; Narcissus; Echo; Pyramus; Thisbe; Medea; Orpheus; and the hundreds of Ovid's figures
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed fourteeners (seven-stress couplets) of tremendous gusto — the metre the Elizabethans read aloud and imitated.
historical_context: The four-book version of 1565 was completed in 1567, in the decade of the Ovidian revival; Shakespeare's allusions to the Metamorphoses — in Midsummer Night's Dream, Titus, and The Tempest — run through this translation.
literary_significance: The English Ovid — the book through which the Renaissance knew its mythology, and the source of a thousand plots, images, and lines.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Seres, 1567. Standard edition: Shakespeare's Ovid, ed. W. H. D. Rouse (1904; repr. 1961).

title: Godfrey of Bulloigne
description: Edward Fairfax's translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata (1581), under the title Godfrey of Bulloigne, or the Recovery of Jerusalem (1600): the crusaders' siege and taking of Jerusalem — Godfrey's command, Rinaldo's enchantment in Armida's garden, Tancred and Clorinda's tragedy — in English ottava rima of grave and musical fidelity, the translation Dryden ranked with the originals.
plot_or_argument: The Christian army besieges Jerusalem; the pagan enchantments of Armida and Ismeno delay the victory; Rinaldo is rescued from the garden of Armida; the duel of Tancred and Clorinda, the battles, and the final assault take the city; and the poem ends with Godfrey's worship at the Sepulchre.
narrative_structure: Twenty cantos of ottava rima following Tasso's order, with Fairfax's 'Allegory of the Poem' appended as the moral key.
principal_characters: Godfrey of Bouillon; Rinaldo; Armida; Tancred; Clorinda; Erminia; Peter the Hermit; Ismeno; Solyman; Argantes
meter_and_prosody: Ottava rima (abababcc) of sustained dignity and sweetness — the metre Fairfax naturalized for English heroic verse.
historical_context: Published 1600, in the decade of the English epic translations (Harington's Ariosto, Sylvester's Du Bartas); Fairfax's Tasso was read by the Spenserians and praised by Dryden as the model of translation.
literary_significance: The great English Tasso — the version through which the Italian romantic epic entered English poetry, and a landmark of translation as an art.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Ar. Hatfield, 1600. Standard edition: Godfrey of Bulloigne, ed. Kathleen M. Lea and T. M. Gang (Oxford, 1981).

title: Du Bartas His Divine Weeks and Works
description: Joshua Sylvester's translation of Guillaume de Saluste du Bartas's biblical epic La Sepmaine: the creation of the world in the 'Divine Weeks', with the vast encyclopedic digressions on natural history, astronomy, and the wonders of the creation — published piecemeal from 1592 and complete in 1608, the most widely read religious poem of its generation after the Bible.
plot_or_argument: The first Week narrates the seven days of creation with their cosmic and natural digressions; the second Week (incomplete in du Bartas) follows the history of the world from Eden toward the redemption; Sylvester's translation renders the whole with a copiousness and inventiveness that made the poem a schoolbook.
narrative_structure: The 'Weeks' of the hexameral tradition — creation and history in epic form, with the translator's dedications and apparatus.
principal_characters: God the Creator; Adam; Eve; the patriarchs; the personified Creation
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed verse of extraordinary lexical invention — Sylvester's coinages and compounds feeding the word-hoard of the next generation.
historical_context: Published in parts from 1592, complete in 1608; du Bartas's poem answered the Huguenot wars with cosmic piety, and Sylvester's version made it the English Protestants' epic, read by the young Milton.
literary_significance: The sacred epic of the English Renaissance — a formative book of the young Milton and the chief English poem of creation before Paradise Lost.
bibliographical_notes: Complete edition, 1608. Standard edition: The Complete Works of Joshua Sylvester, ed. Alexander B. Grosart, 2 vols (1880).

title: The Anatomy of Melancholy
description: Robert Burton's encyclopedic treatise-masquerading-as-self-cure, written under the name 'Democritus Junior': the causes, symptoms, and cures of melancholy anatomized across three 'partitions' — its kinds, its cure, and the special melancholies of love and religion — in a prose of endless quotation, digression, and humane wit, expanded by Burton through five editions to 1651.
plot_or_argument: The First Partition defines melancholy, its causes, and symptoms; the Second prescribes the cures — diet, medicine, mirth, and the consolation of philosophy; the Third anatomizes love-melancholy and religious melancholy, with the great final meditation on despair; the whole is a labyrinth of authorities, stories, and self-portraiture.
narrative_structure: Three partitions with their sections, members, and subsections in the scholastic manner, the apparatus of quotation and marginalia making the book a library in itself.
principal_characters: Democritus Junior (the author's persona); the melancholic patient; the lover; the religious despairer; the quoted authorities
meter_and_prosody: Prose of magnificent copiousness — the style of the study, the pulpit, and the joke fused — with Latin tags and verse interludes.
historical_context: Published 1621, with enlargements in 1624, 1628, 1632, 1638, and posthumously 1651; its melancholy was the century's master-disease, and its book the century's master-digression.
literary_significance: The great English anatomy — the book that taught Sterne, Lamb, and every digressive prose writer since how to wander gloriously.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; published pseudonymously as Democritus Junior.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by John Lichfield, 1621 (six editions to 1651). Standard edition: The Anatomy of Melancholy, ed. Thomas C. Faulkner, Nicolas K. Kiessling, and Rhonda L. Blair, 6 vols (Oxford, 1989–2000).

title: A Survey of London
description: John Stow's loving survey of the capital: London and its liberties described ward by ward, street by street — the walls, gates, churches, schools, markets, conduits, and customs of the city, with its antiquities recovered against the Reformation's destruction and the growth of the Elizabethan metropolis; the foundation of London historiography, enlarged in the 1603 edition.
plot_or_argument: The survey proceeds from the city's Roman origins through the wards of London, then to the suburbs and out-parishes: each church, monument, and custom is given its history, with the old ceremonies and benefactions recorded against oblivion, and the river and its bridges described at the close.
narrative_structure: A topographical description organized by ward and place, in the antiquarian manner of Leland and the chroniclers, with Stow's own memory and reading as its sources.
principal_characters: the city of London itself; its founders, benefactors, and chroniclers
meter_and_prosody: Prose of plain, affectionate exactness — the walker's and rememberer's style.
historical_context: First published 1598 and enlarged in 1603; its record of the pre-Fire city and the pre-Reformation churches is the irreplaceable document of Elizabethan London.
literary_significance: The founding text of London historiography — the book every later historian of the city has built upon, and a classic of English antiquarian prose.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by John Windet, 1598; enlarged 1603. Standard edition: A Survey of London, ed. C. L. Kingsford, 2 vols (Oxford, 1908).

title: Britannia
description: William Camden's chorographical description of Britain, published in Latin in 1586 and enlarged through six editions (the English translation by Philemon Holland appearing in 1610): the island's name, peoples, counties, towns, and antiquities — Roman, Saxon, and medieval — surveyed county by county in the work that founded English antiquarianism and taught the nation its own past.
plot_or_argument: The book proceeds from the general description of Britain and its inhabitants through the counties of England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland: each county's etymology, history, noble families, and antiquities set down with the new documentary scholarship of the age.
narrative_structure: A chorography in the classical tradition (Ptolemy, Pausanias), organized geographically by county, with the apparatus of sources and the author's correspondence as its scholarly frame.
principal_characters: Britain itself; the Britons, Romans, Saxons, and Normans; the noble families and antiquaries
meter_and_prosody: Latin prose of classical elegance (translated by Holland into the full Elizabethan English of 1610).
historical_context: First edition 1586, dedicated to Burghley; Camden's Britannia launched the great tradition of county histories and the Society of Antiquaries' programme, and its 1610 English version made the past accessible to the nation.
literary_significance: The founding work of British antiquarianism — the book that made the island's past a subject of systematic knowledge.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the English translation of 1610 is Philemon Holland's.
bibliographical_notes: First edition, 1586 (six Latin editions to 1607). Standard edition: Britannia, ed. Richard Gough, 4 vols (2nd edn, 1806).

title: Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes
description: Samuel Purchas's four-volume continuation of Hakluyt's collections: the voyage narratives and geographical documents left unpublished at Hakluyt's death — the travels of the East and West Indies, the relations of China and Japan, the Arctic voyages, and the Virginia enterprises — gathered and framed in Purchas's 'pilgrimage' of the world's records, the great Jacobean storehouse of travel literature.
plot_or_argument: No single plot: the Pilgrimes arranges its hundreds of narratives by region and voyage — Purchas's own summaries and moral reflections interlacing the documents — from the voyages of the ancients to the discoveries of his own day.
narrative_structure: Four folio volumes of documentary compilation, with Purchas's prefaces, indices, and the running apparatus of his editorial 'pilgrimage'.
principal_characters: the voyagers and travellers (Hudson, Baffin, Cavendish, and hundreds of others)
meter_and_prosody: Prose of many hands within Purchas's devout editorial frame.
historical_context: Published 1625, the year of Purchas's death and of the Virginia Company's dissolution; the collection preserved many accounts that survive nowhere else and fed the English imagination of empire for two centuries.
literary_significance: The great Jacobean continuation of Hakluyt — the book that carried the age of discovery's records into the age of colonization.
attribution_notes: Compiled and edited by Purchas from Hakluyt's papers and other sources; uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by William Stansby for Henry Fetherstone, 1625. Standard edition: Hakluytus Posthumus, 20 vols (Hakluyt Society, 1905–07).

title: Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum
description: Aemilia Lanyer's volume of sacred poetry, one of the first books of poems published by an Englishwoman: the long title poem on Christ's Passion — with its celebrated 'Eve's Apology' defending women against the blame of the Fall — framed by the eleven dedicatory poems to the great ladies of the court and followed by 'The Description of Cooke-ham', the first country-house poem in English.
plot_or_argument: The Passion poem narrates Christ's betrayal, trial, and crucifixion through the eyes of the women who followed him, with Pilate's wife's dream and the 'Eve's Apology' arguing women's innocence and worth; the dedications praise the Queen, the Countess of Pembroke, and the other patronesses; and Cooke-ham celebrates the estate of Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland, in the farewell of its trees and walks.
narrative_structure: A tripartite volume — dedications, Passion poem, country-house poem — organized as a woman's address to women, the patrons and readers its intended audience.
principal_characters: Christ; Pilate's wife; Eve; the women of Jerusalem; Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland; Anne Clifford; the dedicatees
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal for the Passion poem, with the varied stanzas of the dedications and the elegiac couplets of Cooke-ham.
historical_context: Published 1611, in the year of the King James Bible, by a woman of the court's margins; its argument for women's learning and worth answered the querelle des femmes with theology, and its Cooke-ham preceded Jonson's 'To Penshurst' in the country-house genre.
literary_significance: A founding text of English women's poetry — the first sustained feminist argument in English verse, and the first country-house poem.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Valentine Simmes, 1611. Standard edition: The Poems of Aemilia Lanyer, ed. Susanne Woods (Oxford, 1993).

title: The Countess of Montgomery's Urania
description: Lady Mary Wroth's prose romance, the first by an Englishwoman and a continuation of her uncle Sidney's Arcadia: the interlaced adventures of Pamphilia, Amphilanthus, Urania, and their knights and ladies through the courts and islands of the romance world, with the sonnet sequence 'Pamphilia to Amphilanthus' appended — the book whose recognizable court portraits caused a scandal at its publication.
plot_or_argument: The romance follows the loves of Pamphilia (constant) and Amphilanthus (inconstant), the wanderings of Urania and the shepherds, and the enchanted palaces and rival queens of the romance geography; the appended sonnet sequence tells the same story of constancy and betrayal from Pamphilia's side.
narrative_structure: An interlaced prose romance in the Sidneyan manner, with the sonnet sequence as its lyrical mirror and the author's own family history (the Sidney–Herbert circle) thinly veiled in its portraits.
principal_characters: Pamphilia; Amphilanthus; Urania; Parselius; the romance's queens, shepherds, and enchanters
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the Arcadian school, with the appended sonnets in the Sidneyan form of Wroth's inheritance.
historical_context: Published 1621, dedicated to Susan Herbert, Countess of Montgomery; Sir Edward Denny's furious response to his alleged portrait in the book and Wroth's reply are the first documented quarrel of an English woman novelist with her public.
literary_significance: The first English romance and sonnet sequence by a woman — the foundation of the women's fiction tradition, recovered and canonized by modern scholarship.
bibliographical_notes: Printed for John Marriott and John Grismand, 1621. Standard edition: The First Part of The Countess of Montgomery's Urania, ed. Josephine A. Roberts (Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies, 1995).

title: The Doubt of Future Foes
description: Queen Elizabeth I's poem on Mary Queen of Scots and the succession: the 'doubt of future foes' — the captive rival queen and her foreign allies — threatens the realm, but the poet's 'wit' and providence shall cut off the 'tops of hope' before they grow; the most famous of the queen's surviving poems, circulated in manuscript from the early 1570s.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves from the menace of the rival and her 'foreign banished wights' to the queen's resolve: the sword of justice and the pruning of ambitions — a lyric of statecraft in the register of the mirror-for-princes tradition.
narrative_structure: A single lyric in two movements — the threat, then the answer — in the courtly plain style of the queen's circle.
principal_characters: Elizabeth (as speaker); Mary Queen of Scots (the 'future foe', un-named)
meter_and_prosody: Fourteeners (rhymed seven-stress couplets), the form of the queen's Protestant poetics.
historical_context: Written about 1571, after the Ridolfi plot, when Mary Stuart's captivity and the Catholic powers' intrigues made the succession the realm's danger; it circulated in manuscript and was printed in Puttenham's Art of English Poesy (1589) as the queen's poem.
literary_significance: The queen's own voice in the literature of her reign — the poem through which the sovereign entered the lyric tradition she patronized.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; printed by Puttenham in 1589 as the Queen's.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in George Puttenham, The Art of English Poesy, 1589. Standard edition: Elizabeth I: Collected Works, ed. Leah S. Marcus, Janel Mueller, and Mary Beth Rose (Chicago, 2000).

title: On Monsieur's Departure
description: Queen Elizabeth I's lyric on the departure of François, Duke of Anjou, her last serious suitor, about 1582: the queen's grief at parting, her public duty's compulsion to conceal it, and the paradox of a heart that cannot show what it feels — 'I grieve and dare not show my discontent' — the most personal of her surviving poems.
plot_or_argument: The poem moves through the queen's private grief to the public impossibility of expressing it: love, duty, and statecraft in the single voice of the sovereign, with the refrain of the divided self as its burden.
narrative_structure: A single lyric of three movements — grief, concealment, resignation — in the courtly complaint mode.
principal_characters: Elizabeth (as speaker); the departing Monsieur (François, Duke of Anjou)
meter_and_prosody: Short-lined lyric stanzas with refrain, in the manner of the court's song-poetry.
historical_context: Written about 1582, at the collapse of the French marriage negotiations that had divided the court for a decade; the poem survives only in manuscript, its attribution resting on the queen's circle's testimony.
literary_significance: The queen's most intimate poem — the lyric in which the sovereign's two bodies, private and public, speak in one voice.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Elizabeth I by manuscript tradition; the attribution is generally accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Manuscript only. Standard edition: Elizabeth I: Collected Works, ed. Leah S. Marcus, Janel Mueller, and Mary Beth Rose (Chicago, 2000).
